newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Private Yugoslav petrol firms battle with state.
newsitem.headline: Private Yugoslav petrol firms battle with state.

text.p: A campaign launched by Yugoslav authorities against independent retailers to protect state monopolies has caused petrol shortages for most of the privately-held pumps, industry sources said on Wednesday.
Private firms accused state-run companies of monopolising the market and dictating conditions and prices.

"The private sector is not treated equally. Our demands for import quotas are simply ignored and we are forced to purchase oil derivatives from NIS Jugopetrol and Beopetrol," said an owner of one of Belgrade petrol stations.
"Terms set by Belgrade companies are unfavourable. We lose more than $50 per tonne if we buy from them," he added.
Slavko Nesic, of the private MN company in Loznica, said his company would not have any fuel on the pumps if they did not have long-term joint-investment deal with Belgrade Jugopetrol.
In an attempt to circumvent the monopoly, many dealers turned to Montenegro's Jugopetrol Kotor who offered oil products at lower prices, but fresh problems arose.

"Five of my tankers with fuel purchased from Jugopetrol Kotor are blocked by Serbia's police at the Montenegrin border for no justified reason," said an owner of a petrol station near Pozarevac, some 60 km south-east of Belgrade.
Serbian financial police and the Interior Ministry as well as Yugoslav customs were reported to have been detaining transport vehicles there for hours or even days.

Belgrade officials claimed the control was only a part of wider government action aimed at curbing the grey economy, but politicians say the action is a result of a rift between Serbia and the reformist Montenegrin leadership.
Branko Kascelan of Jugopetrol Kotor, confirmed tankers for private Serbian customers have been sent back from the border.

"Fuel for our Serbian buyers is either held up or sent back from the republics' border for no reason. Meanwhile, the market is thirsty for fuel now due to the summer holiday season and lower production in oil refineries," he said.
"Our prices are from 34 to 45 percent below NIS prices due to our maritime position and vicinity of the port of Bar. Even NIS Jugopetrol buys from us," Kascelan said.

Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, must import crude and refined oil products, such as gasoline, to meet an expecteed domestic products demand of 3.8 million tonnes this year, still 30 percent below the pre-war 1991 level.

Closed off by a rigid United Nations oil and trade embargo from 1992-96, Yugoslavia allowed free imports of products. That led to a doubling of the number of petrol stations to 1,200, of which 500 are private.

Since the lifting of sanctions, the purchases of crude oil abroad were liberalised. But import quotas were set for products to protect two state-run oil refineries now operating with less than half their capacity.
The battle between state-run oil firms and the private sector began in July during a 45-day breakdown in the Pancevo refinery when petrol output dropped to only 1,000 tonnes a day.
The private pumps completely dried up and long queues reappeared at the few regularly-supplied state pumps.

To secure regular supplies, the government early this month raised import quotas for petrol to 130,000 tonnes from 55,000 tonnes, diesel and heating oil to 160,000 tonnes from 100,000 tonnes and primary petrol to 300,000 tonnes from 150,000 tonnes.
NIS Jugopetrol, subsidiary of Serbia's oil and gas company Naftna Industrija Srbije (NIS), and Montenegro's Jugopetrol Kotor were the only two companies authorised to import products.
Belgrade-based Beopetrol, with 200 petrol stations taken over from Croatia's INA after the break up of the old federation in 1992, was only recently allowed of additional quotas.
Analysts linked this move to the posting of a senior official of the Yugoslav Left, a ruling Socialists' coalition partner, as the firm's new manager.
The price for petrol in Serbia is fixed at 3.6 dinars ($0.58) per litre, out of which 0.5 dinars is directed for road reconstruction. Price of diesel fuel is set at 3.0 dinars.
